# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v3-2026-09-22, vocabulary v3-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8
              15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired
              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time
              (greater than 1 is faster)

## The machine this will run on

  cpu model         AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor, 16 core(s) / 32 logical cpu(s), family 25 model 33
  llvm target-cpu   znver3 (what -Ctarget-cpu=native resolves to on this machine)
  isa               avx2, avx, fma, bmi1, bmi2, aes, sha_ni, vaes, vpclmulqdq, popcnt, movbe, rdseed, adx, clwb, clflushopt, erms, fsrm, sse4_2
  no isa            **no AVX-512 of any kind**
  vector width      256 bit, 16 architectural vector registers
                    one register holds 32 x u8, 16 x u16, 8 x u32/f32, 4 x u64/f64
  l1 data           32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l1 instruction    32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l2 unified        512 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l3 unified        32 MiB, 16-way, shared by cpus 0-31
  how it is read    lscpu and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache on this machine, once per run. This is a WSL2 guest: the cache figures are the guest-visible ones and are reported as seen, not corrected.
  how it is timed   the process is pinned to one logical cpu (taskset -c 8) with a 0 ms settle gap between runs, 15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired bootstrap 95% CI

## Where the hints are applied

Function attributes are applied at PipelineStartEP, before any inlining.
Loop metadata is applied at VectorizerStartEP, after inlining and loop
canonicalisation and immediately before LoopVectorize, so a loop hint acts on
the loop as it exists after the function attributes of this same round have
already taken effect.

  113  // driver `hb_k2` does few iterations of heavy work so its block count stays

  119  // the critical path, seventy-odd times per call, and it cannot happen while

criteria.align_64: Set the function's alignment to 64 bytes (`align=64`). The function starts on a cache line. Same mechanism as align=32, one step coarser, and it wastes up to 63 bytes of padding per function.

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v3-2026-09-22, vocabulary v3-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8
              15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired
              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time
              (greater than 1 is faster)

## The machine this will run on

  cpu model         AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor, 16 core(s) / 32 logical cpu(s), family 25 model 33
  llvm target-cpu   znver3 (what -Ctarget-cpu=native resolves to on this machine)
  isa               avx2, avx, fma, bmi1, bmi2, aes, sha_ni, vaes, vpclmulqdq, popcnt, movbe, rdseed, adx, clwb, clflushopt, erms, fsrm, sse4_2
  no isa            **no AVX-512 of any kind**
  vector width      256 bit, 16 architectural vector registers
                    one register holds 32 x u8, 16 x u16, 8 x u32/f32, 4 x u64/f64
  l1 data           32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1

  206  // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

  208  // An integer *add* reduction is throughput-bound --- `vpaddd` has one cycle of
  209  // latency --- so no amount of interleaving can move it. A *multiply* reduction

  211  // accumulator chains is the whole story: at IC 1 the loop retires 8 elements
  212  // every three cycles, at IC 4 it retires 32.

  216  // for any vectorised loop that carries a reduction and never applies the
  217  // small-loop-cost cap to it. So this kernel does not have an `interleave.count`
  218  // winner: it is the site at which the sweep is expected to measure a large
  219  // *loss* for `interleave.count=1` and `=2`, which is what shows that the

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

  242  // target.
  243  //
  244  // Two things keep the function out of line, which `align` needs: a 48-round
  245  // preamble that runs once per call and pushes the inline cost well past any
  246  // threshold a cool call site gets, and two call sites, which deny it the "last
  247  // call to static" bonus. The inner loop does 2^14 iterations per call, so the
  248  // preamble is under a thousandth of the kernel's work.

  253      hb_rounds!(
  254          h, 0x2f, 0x4b, 0x61, 0x7d, 0x93, 0xa9, 0xbf, 0xd5, 0xeb, 0x0f, 0x21,

  - attributes already on it: (none)
  - inliner mechanics of this recipe: with a profile present, `inlinehint` and `cold` on a function do not change the inliner's threshold for it, because the call site's own hotness class assigns that threshold afterwards; `alwaysinline` and `noinline` are decided before the cost model runs and are always honoured

criteria.KEEP_DEFAULT: Change nothing about this function's attributes. This is the 'no change' option: the build keeps whatever LLVM's own cost model decides, exactly as in the baseline.
criteria.inline_always: Add the `alwaysinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(always)`). The body is pasted into every call site, whatever the inliner's cost model would have decided: the choice is made before any cost is computed, so a call site's measured hotness cannot overrule it. It tends to help a small hot leaf (roughly under 300 instructions) that the inliner is declining to paste in, because the caller then specialises on what it passes and the call overhead goes away. It tends to hurt a large body (a thousand instructions and up) and a function with many monomorphized copies, since every call site pays the full code growth with no cost model left to stop it. Where inlining is impossible --- a recursive self-call, a target-feature mismatch --- nothing happens and the build says so with a `NotInlined` remark. It is a no-op where every call site was being inlined anyway.
criteria.inline_never: Add the `noinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(never)`). The function stays one out-of-line copy: call overhead is paid at every call site and the callers stay small. Like `alwaysinline` it is decided before the cost model runs, so the profile cannot overrule it either. It tends to help a very large body (thousands of instructions) or a function with many monomorphized copies, by stopping code growth and instruction-cache pressure --- especially where an `inlinehint` is already asking the inliner to paste that body in. It tends to hurt a small hot leaf, where the call overhead is the bulk of the cost. It is a no-op where the body is already too large for any caller's threshold.
criteria.align_16: Set the function's alignment to 16 bytes (the SPEC vocabulary's `align=16`). This is the usual default on x86-64, so it mostly means 'pin the current alignment'.
criteria.align_32: Set the function's alignment to 32 bytes (`align=32`). The entry point starts on a 32-byte boundary, which changes how the function's first instructions and its first loop fall into the 32-byte instruction-fetch windows and the uop cache.
criteria.align_64: Set the function's alignment to 64 bytes (`align=64`). The function starts on a cache line. Same mechanism as align=32, one step coarser, and it wastes up to 63 bytes of padding per function.

# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v3-2026-09-22, vocabulary v3-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8
              15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired
              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time
              (greater than 1 is faster)

## The machine this will run on

  cpu model         AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor, 16 core(s) / 32 logical cpu(s), family 25 model 33
  llvm target-cpu   znver3 (what -Ctarget-cpu=native resolves to on this machine)
  isa               avx2, avx, fma, bmi1, bmi2, aes, sha_ni, vaes, vpclmulqdq, popcnt, movbe, rdseed, adx, clwb, clflushopt, erms, fsrm, sse4_2
  no isa            **no AVX-512 of any kind**
  vector width      256 bit, 16 architectural vector registers
                    one register holds 32 x u8, 16 x u16, 8 x u32/f32, 4 x u64/f64
  l1 data           32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l1 instruction    32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l2 unified        512 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1

  103  // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  104  // K2 --- inline: a leaf just over the default inline threshold
  105  // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  106  //
  107  // `inlinehint` replaces the base threshold 250 with 325 and the single-basic-
  108  // block and vector bonuses scale from there, so it moves a call site's
  109  // threshold by about 30% and nothing more. The only leaf it can flip is one
  110  // whose cost lands inside that 30% window, at a call site the profile does not
  111  // call hot. Both are engineered: the round count below is chosen from the
  112  // measured `(cost=..., threshold=...)` remark of the baseline build, and the
  113  // driver `hb_k2` does few iterations of heavy work so its block count stays
  114  // three orders of magnitude under the vectorised kernels'.
  115  //
  116  // What inlining buys beyond the call itself: `mode` is a constant at both call
  117  // sites, so the register multiply in every round becomes a multiply by 5 and
  118  // the backend turns it into an `lea`. That is a two-cycle saving per round on
  119  // the critical path, seventy-odd times per call, and it cannot happen while
  120  // the callee is a separate function.
  121  
  122  macro_rules! k2_round {
  123      ($v:ident, $m:ident, $k:literal) => {
  124          $v = $v.wrapping_mul($m).rotate_left(5) ^ ($k as u32);
  125      };
  126  }
  127  
  128  macro_rules! k2_rounds {
  129      ($v:ident, $m:ident, $($k:literal),* $(,)?) => { $( k2_round!($v, $m, $k); )* };
  130  }
  131  
  132  /// Leaf mixer for K2. Marked; the hint under test is `inline`.
  133  ///
  134  /// `m` is derived from `mode`, which is a constant at both call sites. Out of
  135  /// line, every round pays a register `imul` (three cycles on znver3); inlined,
  136  /// `m` folds to 5 and the multiply becomes an `lea` (one cycle). That is where
  137  /// the win is: the inline cost model counts the multiply the same either way,
  138  /// so making the argument constant does not push the callee back under the
  139  /// threshold, and the strength reduction only happens after inlining.
  140 >pub fn k2_mix(x: u32, mode: u32, rot: u32) -> u32 {
  141      let m = (mode & 7) | 1;
  142      let mut v = x ^ rot;
  143      k2_rounds!(
  144          v, m, 0xba, 0x33, 0x82, 0xab, 0xca, 0xa3, 0x92, 0x1b, 0xda, 0x13,
  145          0xa2, 0x8b, 0xea, 0x83, 0xb2, 0xfb, 0xfa, 0xf3, 0xc2, 0x6b, 0x0a,
  146          0x63, 0xd2, 0xdb, 0x1a, 0xd3, 0xe2, 0x4b, 0x2a, 0x43, 0xf2, 0xbb,
  147          0x3a, 0xb3, 0x02, 0x2b, 0x4a, 0x23, 0x12, 0x9b, 0x5a, 0x93, 0x22,
  148          0x0b, 0x6a, 0x03, 0x32, 0x7b, 0x7a, 0x73, 0x42, 0xeb, 0x8a, 0xe3,
  149          0x52, 0x5b, 0x9a, 0x53, 0x62, 0xcb,
  150      );
  151      v ^ (v >> 7)
  152  }

  154  // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  155  // K3 --- unroll.disable: the zopfli cache.rs:108 shape
  156  // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  157  //
  158  // A `while i <= end` fill over a slice with a runtime trip count of 4 to 19.
  159  // The rotate carried from one iteration to the next is what keeps the
  160  // vectoriser out ("value that could not be identified as reduction"): a plain
  161  // fill of a constant is vectorised at width 16 here, which on a trip count of
  162  // a dozen means the vector body never runs and the loop pays the guard for
  163  // nothing. With the vectoriser out of the way the unroller is the only thing
  164  // left that a hint can reach, and its default runtime unroll pays a prologue
  165  // and an epilogue for a loop that runs a dozen times (decision 22: on zopfli's
  166  // version of this loop, turning the unroll off was worth +1.6%).
  167  
  168  /// Fill `dst[prev..=end]` with a rotating value. Marked; the hint under test
  169  /// is `unroll.disable` on its single loop.
  170  pub fn k3_fill_run(dst: &mut [u16], prev: usize, end: usize, dist: u16) -> u16 {
  171      let mut i = prev;
  172      let mut v = dist;
  173      while i <= end {
  174          dst[i] = v;
  175          v = v.rotate_left(3) ^ 0x9E37;
  176          i += 1;
  177      }
  178      v
  179  }

  248  // preamble is under a thousandth of the kernel's work.

## Where the hints are applied

Function attributes are applied at PipelineStartEP, before any inlining.
Loop metadata is applied at VectorizerStartEP, after inlining and loop
canonicalisation and immediately before LoopVectorize, so a loop hint acts on
the loop as it exists after the function attributes of this same round have
already taken effect.

criteria.inline_always: Add the `alwaysinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(always)`). It tends to help a small hot leaf (roughly under 300 instructions) that the inliner is declining to paste in, because the caller then specialises on what it passes and the call overhead goes away. It tends to hurt a large body (a thousand instructions and up) and a function with many monomorphized copies, since every call site pays the full code growth with no cost model left to stop it. It is a no-op where every call site was being inlined anyway.
criteria.inline_never: Add the `noinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(never)`). The function stays one out-of-line copy: call overhead is paid at every call site and the callers stay small. It tends to help a very large body (thousands of instructions) or a function with many monomorphized copies, by stopping code growth and instruction-cache pressure --- especially where an `inlinehint` is already asking the inliner to paste that body in. It tends to hurt a small hot leaf, where the call overhead is the bulk of the cost. It is a no-op where the body is already too large for any caller's threshold.
criteria.align_16: Set the function's alignment to 16 bytes (the SPEC vocabulary's `align=16`). This is the usual default on x86-64, so it mostly means 'pin the current alignment'.
criteria.align_32: Set the function's alignment to 32 bytes (`align=32`). The entry point starts on a 32-byte boundary, which changes how the function's first instructions and its first loop fall into the 32-byte instruction-fetch windows and the uop cache.
criteria.align_64: Set the function's alignment to 64 bytes (`align=64`). The function starts on a cache line. Same mechanism as align=32, one step coarser, and it wastes up to 63 bytes of padding per function.

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

The body is pasted into every call site, whatever the inliner's cost model would have decided: the choice is made before any cost is computed, so a call site's measured hotness cannot overrule it. It tends to help a small hot leaf (roughly under 300 instructions) that the inliner is declining to paste in, because the caller then specialises on what it passes and the call overhead goes away. It tends to hurt a large body (a thousand instructions and up) and a function with many monomorphized copies, since every call site pays the full code growth with no cost model left to stop it. criteria.align_64: Set the function's alignment to 64 bytes (`align=64`). The function starts on a cache line. Same mechanism as align=32, one step coarser, and it wastes up to 63 bytes of padding per function.

# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v3-2026-09-22, vocabulary v3-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8
              15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired
              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time
              (greater than 1 is faster)

  cpu model         AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor, 16 core(s) / 32 logical cpu(s), family 25 model 33
  llvm target-cpu   znver3 (what -Ctarget-cpu=native resolves to on this machine)

criteria.KEEP_DEFAULT: Attach no metadata to this loop. This is the 'no change' option: LLVM's vectoriser and unroller decide with their own cost model, exactly as in the baseline.
criteria.unroll_count_2: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 2`: unroll the loop body twice. Halves the loop-control overhead and gives the scheduler two iterations to interleave. Note that this runs after vectorisation, so on a loop LLVM vectorises it unrolls the *vector* loop.
criteria.unroll_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 4`: unroll the loop body four times. More scheduling freedom and fewer branches than count=2, at four times the body's code size and a longer remainder loop.
criteria.unroll_count_8: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 8`: unroll the loop body eight times. Only worth it for a very short body with a high trip count; otherwise the code growth costs more in instruction cache than the saved branches are worth.
criteria.unroll_disable: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.disable`: forbid unrolling this loop entirely. Keeps the body small, which helps when the loop is short and unpredictable or when the caller's instruction footprint is the problem.
criteria.vectorize_width_2: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 2` (and `vectorize.enable`): force two lanes per vector iteration. A narrow forced width is a way to keep vectorisation but cut the cost of the scalar remainder when the trip count is low. Reassociation of floating-point reductions stays forbidden (the build pins -hints-allow-reordering=false), so a non-reassociable reduction will simply not be widened.
criteria.vectorize_width_4: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 4` (and `vectorize.enable`): four lanes per vector iteration. On this machine (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512) that is one 256-bit register for 64-bit elements.
criteria.vectorize_width_8: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 8` (and `vectorize.enable`): eight lanes per vector iteration. For 32-bit elements that is one 256-bit register; for 64-bit elements it is two, which LLVM will split.
criteria.vectorize_width_16: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 16` (and `vectorize.enable`): sixteen lanes per vector iteration. Only 8-bit and 16-bit element types fit that in one AVX2 register; for anything wider LLVM emits several registers per iteration, which can pay off on a very long loop and hurts on a short one.
criteria.interleave_count_1: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 1`: vectorise without interleaving, i.e. one vector body per iteration and a single accumulator chain. Shortens the loop and the remainder when LLVM's default interleaving was too aggressive.
criteria.interleave_count_2: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 2`: two independent vector chains per iteration, which hides the latency of a dependent reduction at the cost of more registers.
criteria.interleave_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 4`: four independent vector chains per iteration. The most latency hiding of the three and the most register pressure; on a short trip count the remainder loop eats the gain.

# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v3-2026-09-22, vocabulary v3-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core

              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8

              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time

criteria.KEEP_DEFAULT: Change nothing about this function's attributes. This is the 'no change' option: the build keeps whatever LLVM's own cost model decides, exactly as in the baseline.
criteria.inline_always: Add the `alwaysinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(always)`). The body is pasted into every call site, whatever the inliner's cost model would have decided: the choice is made before any cost is computed, so a call site's measured hotness cannot overrule it. It tends to help a small hot leaf (roughly under 300 instructions) that the inliner is declining to paste in, because the caller then specialises on what it passes and the call overhead goes away. It tends to hurt a large body (a thousand instructions and up) and a function with many monomorphized copies, since every call site pays the full code growth with no cost model left to stop it. Where inlining is impossible --- a recursive self-call, a target-feature mismatch --- nothing happens and the build says so with a `NotInlined` remark. It is a no-op where every call site was being inlined anyway.
criteria.inline_never: Add the `noinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(never)`). The function stays one out-of-line copy: call overhead is paid at every call site and the callers stay small. Like `alwaysinline` it is decided before the cost model runs, so the profile cannot overrule it either. It tends to help a very large body (thousands of instructions) or a function with many monomorphized copies, by stopping code growth and instruction-cache pressure --- especially where an `inlinehint` is already asking the inliner to paste that body in. It tends to hurt a small hot leaf, where the call overhead is the bulk of the cost. It is a no-op where the body is already too large for any caller's threshold.
criteria.align_16: Set the function's alignment to 16 bytes (the SPEC vocabulary's `align=16`). This is the usual default on x86-64, so it mostly means 'pin the current alignment'.
criteria.align_32: Set the function's alignment to 32 bytes (`align=32`). The entry point starts on a 32-byte boundary, which changes how the function's first instructions and its first loop fall into the 32-byte instruction-fetch windows and the uop cache.
criteria.align_64: Set the function's alignment to 64 bytes (`align=64`). The function starts on a cache line. Same mechanism as align=32, one step coarser, and it wastes up to 63 bytes of padding per function.

# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v3-2026-09-22, vocabulary v3-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8
              15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired
              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time
              (greater than 1 is faster)

## The machine this will run on

  cpu model         AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor, 16 core(s) / 32 logical cpu(s), family 25 model 33
  llvm target-cpu   znver3 (what -Ctarget-cpu=native resolves to on this machine)
  isa               avx2, avx, fma, bmi1, bmi2, aes, sha_ni, vaes, vpclmulqdq, popcnt, movbe, rdseed, adx, clwb, clflushopt, erms, fsrm, sse4_2
  no isa            **no AVX-512 of any kind**
  vector width      256 bit, 16 architectural vector registers
                    one register holds 32 x u8, 16 x u16, 8 x u32/f32, 4 x u64/f64
  l1 data           32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1

Function attributes are applied at PipelineStartEP, before any inlining.

canonicalisation and immediately before LoopVectorize, so a loop hint acts on
the loop as it exists after the function attributes of this same round have

criteria.unroll_count_2: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 2`: unroll the loop body twice. Halves the loop-control overhead and gives the scheduler two iterations to interleave. Note that this runs after vectorisation, so on a loop LLVM vectorises it unrolls the *vector* loop.
criteria.unroll_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 4`: unroll the loop body four times. More scheduling freedom and fewer branches than count=2, at four times the body's code size and a longer remainder loop.
criteria.unroll_count_8: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 8`: unroll the loop body eight times. Only worth it for a very short body with a high trip count; otherwise the code growth costs more in instruction cache than the saved branches are worth.
criteria.unroll_disable: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.disable`: forbid unrolling this loop entirely. Keeps the body small, which helps when the loop is short and unpredictable or when the caller's instruction footprint is the problem.
criteria.vectorize_width_2: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 2` (and `vectorize.enable`): force two lanes per vector iteration. A narrow forced width is a way to keep vectorisation but cut the cost of the scalar remainder when the trip count is low. Reassociation of floating-point reductions stays forbidden (the build pins -hints-allow-reordering=false), so a non-reassociable reduction will simply not be widened.
criteria.vectorize_width_4: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 4` (and `vectorize.enable`): four lanes per vector iteration. On this machine (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512) that is one 256-bit register for 64-bit elements.
criteria.vectorize_width_8: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 8` (and `vectorize.enable`): eight lanes per vector iteration. For 32-bit elements that is one 256-bit register; for 64-bit elements it is two, which LLVM will split.
criteria.vectorize_width_16: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 16` (and `vectorize.enable`): sixteen lanes per vector iteration. Only 8-bit and 16-bit element types fit that in one AVX2 register; for anything wider LLVM emits several registers per iteration, which can pay off on a very long loop and hurts on a short one.
criteria.interleave_count_1: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 1`: vectorise without interleaving, i.e. one vector body per iteration and a single accumulator chain. Shortens the loop and the remainder when LLVM's default interleaving was too aggressive.
criteria.interleave_count_2: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 2`: two independent vector chains per iteration, which hides the latency of a dependent reduction at the cost of more registers.
criteria.interleave_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 4`: four independent vector chains per iteration. The most latency hiding of the three and the most register pressure; on a short trip count the remainder loop eats the gain.

# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v3-2026-09-22, vocabulary v3-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core

              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false

              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time

criteria.KEEP_DEFAULT: Change nothing about this function's attributes. This is the 'no change' option: the build keeps whatever LLVM's own cost model decides, exactly as in the baseline.
criteria.inline_always: Add the `alwaysinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(always)`). The body is pasted into every call site, whatever the inliner's cost model would have decided: the choice is made before any cost is computed, so a call site's measured hotness cannot overrule it. It tends to help a small hot leaf (roughly under 300 instructions) that the inliner is declining to paste in, because the caller then specialises on what it passes and the call overhead goes away. It tends to hurt a large body (a thousand instructions and up) and a function with many monomorphized copies, since every call site pays the full code growth with no cost model left to stop it. Where inlining is impossible --- a recursive self-call, a target-feature mismatch --- nothing happens and the build says so with a `NotInlined` remark. It is a no-op where every call site was being inlined anyway.
criteria.inline_never: Add the `noinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(never)`). The function stays one out-of-line copy: call overhead is paid at every call site and the callers stay small. Like `alwaysinline` it is decided before the cost model runs, so the profile cannot overrule it either. It tends to help a very large body (thousands of instructions) or a function with many monomorphized copies, by stopping code growth and instruction-cache pressure --- especially where an `inlinehint` is already asking the inliner to paste that body in. It tends to hurt a small hot leaf, where the call overhead is the bulk of the cost. It is a no-op where the body is already too large for any caller's threshold.
criteria.align_16: Set the function's alignment to 16 bytes (the SPEC vocabulary's `align=16`). This is the usual default on x86-64, so it mostly means 'pin the current alignment'.
criteria.align_32: Set the function's alignment to 32 bytes (`align=32`). The entry point starts on a 32-byte boundary, which changes how the function's first instructions and its first loop fall into the 32-byte instruction-fetch windows and the uop cache.
criteria.align_64: Set the function's alignment to 64 bytes (`align=64`). The function starts on a cache line. Same mechanism as align=32, one step coarser, and it wastes up to 63 bytes of padding per function.

Mechanical readings for this site. Each line is produced by a tool from the numbers and the compiler remarks already in the state, by the same rule at every site in this request; none of them is an opinion about which hint to choose.
  - body size: 14 LLVM instructions after LTO
  - size class: tiny (rule: <50 tiny, <300 small, <1000 medium, <2000 large, >=2000 very large)
  - distinct copies in the binary: 1 monomorphization(s); copy class single (rule: 1 single, 2-8 few, >=9 many)
  - inline budget: LLVM's defaults are -inline-threshold=225 and -inlinehint-threshold=325 cost units; body instructions / -inline-threshold=225 = 0.1x, i.e. the body fits inside that budget (an order-of-magnitude comparison, not an InlineCost computation --- the cost=/threshold= pairs in the remarks above are the real ones, and they are about this function's callees)
  - attributes already on it: (none)
  - inliner mechanics of this recipe: with a profile present, `inlinehint` and `cold` on a function do not change the inliner's threshold for it, because the call site's own hotness class assigns that threshold afterwards; `alwaysinline` and `noinline` are decided before the cost model runs and are always honoured
  - share of the program's user cycles: 12.50%; hotness class very hot (rule: <1% not hot, 1-5% hot, >=5% very hot)
  - loop sites inside it: 1 (`loop_in_mark` sites of this mark in the dump)

criteria.KEEP_DEFAULT: Change nothing about this function's attributes. This is the 'no change' option: the build keeps whatever LLVM's own cost model decides, exactly as in the baseline.
criteria.inline_always: Add the `alwaysinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(always)`). The body is pasted into every call site, whatever the inliner's cost model would have decided: the choice is made before any cost is computed, so a call site's measured hotness cannot overrule it. It tends to help a small hot leaf (roughly under 300 instructions) that the inliner is declining to paste in, because the caller then specialises on what it passes and the call overhead goes away. It tends to hurt a large body (a thousand instructions and up) and a function with many monomorphized copies, since every call site pays the full code growth with no cost model left to stop it. Where inlining is impossible --- a recursive self-call, a target-feature mismatch --- nothing happens and the build says so with a `NotInlined` remark. It is a no-op where every call site was being inlined anyway.
criteria.inline_never: Add the `noinline` attribute (the SPEC vocabulary's `inline(never)`). The function stays one out-of-line copy: call overhead is paid at every call site and the callers stay small. Like `alwaysinline` it is decided before the cost model runs, so the profile cannot overrule it either. It tends to help a very large body (thousands of instructions) or a function with many monomorphized copies, by stopping code growth and instruction-cache pressure --- especially where an `inlinehint` is already asking the inliner to paste that body in. It tends to hurt a small hot leaf, where the call overhead is the bulk of the cost. It is a no-op where the body is already too large for any caller's threshold.
criteria.align_16: Set the function's alignment to 16 bytes (the SPEC vocabulary's `align=16`). This is the usual default on x86-64, so it mostly means 'pin the current alignment'.
criteria.align_32: Set the function's alignment to 32 bytes (`align=32`). The entry point starts on a 32-byte boundary, which changes how the function's first instructions and its first loop fall into the 32-byte instruction-fetch windows and the uop cache.
criteria.align_64: Set the function's alignment to 64 bytes (`align=64`). The function starts on a cache line. Same mechanism as align=32, one step coarser, and it wastes up to 63 bytes of padding per function.
